utterances.text: There were people who did that, but I don't know who the individuals were because these were not people from my village or one of the villages closer to mine. I didn't know someone from Zvornik, Zepa, or Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And even though you didn't know them, the persons who might have done that, do you know whether they went through the terrain between whatever place or town that they got the materials from back to Srebrenica not using the main roads?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no free town anywhere near Srebrenica. One could go to the nearby villages and to use the main road or through the fields or woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior -- when you were in the construction business prior to the war, did you ever have to make an order for timber to be cut in order to have building materials?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times, and I still do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the area that the timber came from, was that within the Bratunac municipality and the Srebrenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That timber wasn't coming in during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I certainly understand that. I'm speaking about prior to the war, if I can just turn your attention there briefly.

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a sawmill, a state-owned sawmill in the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you also: In terms of living in Srebrenica and doing this construction work, was there any type of informal market place where one could exchange building materials for other building materials, depending on what they needed?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I do understand that you did mention that there seemed to be an exchange that could occur between people in Srebrenica as it related to food. That was your testimony, wasn't it, Mr. Tiro?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you've testified that on more than one occasion that you took rakija, which is a plum brandy if I understand, and honey in order to exchange it in this informal market in Srebrenica. Isn't that your testimony, Mr. Rakija -- I'm sorry, Mr. Tiro?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The witness never mentioned a market place. He did mention exchange or a trade off but not a market place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question does not refer to a market place. It says, at least according to the transcript: "In this informal market, informal market," that's what we have in the English transcript. I don't know how it was translated into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was interpreted as I said. That confused me and it probably confused the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So it should be clear to the witness now. We are referring to an informal market, informal bartering system that is being suggested to you existed in Srebrenica. I hope I haven't confused the matter further by using the word "barter."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tiro, can we just confirm that there was an informal exchange in between people regarding food that we refer to here as a bartering system or informal market.

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was exchange. If I say brought some rakija, I could exchange it for flour or vegetables that I needed. If someone lived in the country, they could bring some plums, apples, vegetables, and they could exchange that for flour because nobody had any money to be able to use it or profit from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was rakija a commodity that was fairly valuable on this informal -- in this informal exchange situation?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was of value, if there was any. That's the survival in any which way possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking specifically -- I understand your response, but I'm asking specifically for rakija because I understand on two occasions that you took rakija and honey in order to use in the exchange. Is that because it was a valuable commodity in particular?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the only thing I found. Had I found any flour I wouldn't have taken rakija or had I found any grain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Question -- I think again there may be a hitch here. The question as I understood it is as follows: Was there a demand for rakija in this informal market setting existing at the time in Srebrenica? Was there a demand for rakija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Rakija was not in demand, but someone did need that as I needed wheat or flour or potatoes, whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, at times I imagine you would get wheat and flour for your exchange of rakija or honey. Would you just tell the Trial Chamber where this informal market place took place in Srebrenica, if anywhere.

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would go in the country trying to go through the free Muslim villages because they did grow something, they sowed, harvested, a few villages towards Suceska. And then one could trade with those people. And sometimes they helped of their own accord without any exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that this informal exchange took place outside of Srebrenica within the Muslim villages when you would leave Srebrenica and go to the villages. Is that what I'm understanding?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would go to the free villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there any place in Srebrenica in the city, in the town, where people would gather to exchange food items?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a small one. It wasn't a market, it was just simply a place on the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us in what part of Srebrenica that was.

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was up towards Petrici and Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this take place in the morning or the afternoon of a given day?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no specific time when the women had some cheese or soft cheese, kajmak, to exchange for something, or milk. That's when they would have these kinds of foods that were most likely to the exchanged in Srebrenica where there were a lot of people who didn't have a cow or anything. It was the only way that you could get some cheese, hard cheese, soft cheese, milk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, it was mainly the women who would go to this place near Petrici to exchange the food?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, I'm assuming that you were also indicating that this could take place on any day during the week and any time during the day?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tiro, you were in Srebrenica in the first two weeks of August, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the 8th of August and the 15th of August, did any of the women in your family tell you or did you come to know that the activity at this informal market place increased because there was either a higher level of food or just new items that had been brought in?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody said anything like that and I didn't see that for myself. I didn't have time to go and see what anybody in Srebrenica was doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because at this time period you were busy constructing the houses. Is that the reason you couldn't go to the market and see whether new food had arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer, Mr. Tiro, please, because the interpreters could not catch up with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My previous answer, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I repeat to you the question that Ms. Sellers -- and then you repeat the answer, please. "Because at this time period you were busy constructing the houses. Is that the reason you couldn't go to the market and see whether new food had arrived?" And you gave a very short answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not because of the houses. I wasn't interested actually in what was going on in the street. I had my own problems regarding these exchanges and the market [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tiro, might I ask you what you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I take it there has been some mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, Your Honour. In the transcript he said "I had my own problems even without this exchange and the market." Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It does make a difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic, for that. It certainly does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tiro, can you ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- how often, if at all, during July and August did you go to the market place?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Srebrenica you arrived with some family members who were women or girls. Did they ever go to the market during 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't even allow them to go there because it was dangerous. A lot of shells hit Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know of the existence and the functioning of this market from information from whom, Mr. Tiro?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a market place. I said it was a place just on the street. A market is a market; that's something else. An open market would have to have its stalls and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, certainly we're not talking about that. We'll go back to a place of exchange. But we're referring to what you testified previously Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about that place of exchange. You heard about that or learned about its existence and functioning from whom?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who did I hear about it from? Well, I heard it from people. I'm going there to exchange that for milk, to exchange this for cheese. People would go and exchange that because that was the safest place you could take cover behind the cultural hall and those other buildings there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to your knowledge was there a warehouse in Srebrenica where food was stored or any place that was used, particularly in July, August, September, October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of food would be stored and who would store it when there was no food until humanitarian aid started reaching Srebrenica and even that were small quantities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tiro, I'm referring to any food that might have come in in the intervening time, but let's go to the humanitarian aid. Would you agree with me that that aid arrived in November or early December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you present in Srebrenica when the aid arrived?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was when I went to bury a relative of mine who was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you heard that the aid was coming to Srebrenica at that time period, prior to your having to unfortunately bury a family member?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't know anything about that, that it would come and when it would come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if I understand you correctly, when you're saying "we didn't know anything about that," are you referring to your family members, to the extended family members, are you referring to the refugee population in general didn't know that the aid was coming?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know what others knew. I am just speaking about myself and my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that there had been demands made in Srebrenica for humanitarian convoys to come with the welcome relief of food?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I wasn't really involved in that or I didn't think about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did any of your family members go down and physically receive any humanitarian aid when it arrived?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What would they physically receive? This was distributed by people. They all knew that they were entitled to receive a part of it. Nobody took food from anyone else. There were people at the time who were responsible for distributing this humanitarian aid to everybody equally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your testimony is then that your family members or those receiving this equal distribution were going to receive it after it had been delivered in Srebrenica. Is that what I understand you to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer first and then we'll -- I know what you're coming up with, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no family could receive it before the humanitarian aid arrived. So when the humanitarian aid started to arrive, that's when it was received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this will assist the Prosecutor also. Perhaps they could pose a simple question because when the Prosecutor said "did the family physically receive it" in the spirit of our language and I saw the witness understand it that way, it meant: Did anybody seize it or grab it from somebody else. Is that so, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So perhaps the Prosecutor could ask a more simple question so that the witness could be and clear understand it clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm quite grateful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would never intend to mean that your family seized it in the English sense. Let me say did anyone in your family physically receive -- was it handed to them willingly and voluntarily on the day or the time period when the humanitarian aid arrived?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was given to them willingly and they of course brought it home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber where was it in terms of the place in Srebrenica that this humanitarian aid arrived, in what part of the town?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the centre, the centre of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your family members were at the centre when it arrived or they were informed that it had arrived and then proceeded to the centre?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were all called. The people were called to come so that they could receive food in order to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Could you explain to me in what manner were they called, meaning how -- what instrument was used to call them or was it -- how were they informed?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said before that a group was formed, a group of people who were going to honestly distribute it to everybody. So those people called all the people, not at once but according to a certain order so that everyone received their share of the food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tiro. That does clarify it for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And my last question, Your Honours, for today is:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This group of people that was formed were people who were in Srebrenica, is this correct, prior to the convoy or the humanitarian aid coming?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't only the people from Srebrenica who worked there. There were people from Bratunac and Zepa who also worked there as well as from Vlasenica. They put four or five people in charge of dealing with that humanitarian aid so that everybody would receive an equal share.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you refer to "they put the people in charge," who is the "they," those who were responsible; do you know?

utterances.speaker: HAMED TIRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that they were placed in charge but they kind of made themselves, declared themselves as people in charge. I don't know who -- how this was formed. I mean, I myself didn't have the opportunity to go to meetings or anything like that, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tiro, you've been quite informative today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you very much, Ms. Sellers. We will stop here for today. Mr. Tiro, we will continue in the morning. In the meantime, take good rest and make sure, please, that you do not allow anyone to communicate with you on matters related to your evidence and that you yourself will not try to communicate with anyone on the same matters. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
